title: Newton's law of gravitation and field strength; Electric field strength and field lines
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: C03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; C03-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; C03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; F03-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: C03-1#N.3, F03-1#N.2, C03-1#N.8a, F03-1#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Gravitational field strength
items.clue: Force per unit mass on a small test mass, in N kg⁻¹.

items.label: Uniform field
items.clue: Model used near the surface, where g barely changes.

items.label: Inverse-square law
items.clue: Pattern in which doubling r divides the pull by four.

items.label: Neutral point
items.clue: Place between two like charges where E = 0, nearer the smaller one.

questions.stem: Two objects exert gravitational forces of magnitude F on each other. The mass of each object is doubled, and the distance between their centres is tripled. What is the new magnitude of the gravitational force that each object exerts on the other?

At point P, a charge of +2.0 µC experiences an electric force of 5.0 × 10⁻³ N directed east. This charge is removed and a charge of −6.0 µC is placed at P; the charges that produce the field do not move. Taking east as positive, what is the electric force on the −6.0 µC charge?

The Earth exerts a gravitational force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. The mass of the Moon is about 1.2% of the mass of the Earth. Which statement about the gravitational force that the Moon exerts on the Earth is correct?

options.text: It is 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, and it pulls the Earth towards the Moon.
It is about 1.2% of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, as the Moon has far less mass.
It is zero, as a small body cannot attract a much larger one.
It is zero, as the Moon has no air and so has no gravity.

questions.stem: The field lines of a long, straight charged wire spread out radially, in planes at right angles to the wire: they spread in two dimensions, not three. Point P is 2.0 cm from the wire and point Q is 6.0 cm from it, both far from the wire's ends. How does the electric field strength at P compare with that at Q?

options.text: E at P is 9 times E at Q, as the field strength falls with the square of the distance.
E at P is 3 times E at Q, as the same lines spread over 3 times the area at Q.
E is the same at P and Q, as every line that passes P also passes Q.
E at Q is 3 times E at P, as the larger cylinder at Q holds more lines.
